title: Money and happiness
hookLine: researchers who disagreed ran a joint study and found happiness mostly keeps rising with income, except for the least happy
last: WE ADAPT, OFTEN MORE THAN WE EXPECT.

cards: Does money buy happiness? Two serious researchers gave two different answers. Daniel Kahneman, with the economist Angus Deaton, had found that day-to-day happiness seemed to level off above a certain income.
Another researcher, Matthew Killingsworth, using a different method, found it kept rising. They could have kept answering each other in print.
Instead they sat down together, with a third researcher as referee, and went looking for the truth in the same data.

teach.b: First, the method. Killingsworth, Kahneman and the psychologist Barbara Mellers published their joint work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
It's called an adversarial collaboration: people who disagree design the test together, so nobody can stack the deck. Second, the finding.
For most people, day-to-day happiness kept rising as income rose, with no clear ceiling. But the rise works in proportion: the same raise means more to someone with less.
Third, the exception, and it's what reconciled the two camps.

teach.h: FOR THE LEAST HAPPY, IT FLATTENS.
teach.b: For the least happy group, happiness rose with income only up to a point, then flattened.

The authors suggest that for those people, the deepest sources of misery, like grief, heartbreak or depression, aren't things a bigger paycheck can fix. Money helps a lot of things. It doesn't reach everything.
Fourth, an old warning that fits. In the Gospel of Luke, someone asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute with his brother.
Jesus declines, and says, in the King James Bible: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."
The Greek word behind covetousness is pleonexia, the grasping for more. He doesn't say money is meaningless. He says life doesn't consist in it.
That's close to where the data landed.

how: Some people pair practical care about money with a habit of naming what it can't buy, an idea scripture voices too, as in Jesus's warning in Luke about covetousness.

games.q: you've published a finding, and a respected colleague has published the opposite. what do you do?
o: write a sharper paper attacking theirs.
design a new study together, with a referee.
games.why: Killingsworth and Kahneman did exactly that, with Barbara Mellers. the result explained both earlier findings.

practice: Without judging money at all, let your mind go to the things in your life no amount of it could buy: someone's trust, a sibling's old joke, your child's handwriting, a night of real rest, the way a certain friend says your name.
Let one come forward, and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Money and happiness. For most people they rise together, steadily. For the least happy, money helps only up to a point. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, in Luke 12:15, rendered 'covetousness' in the King James Bible: the grasping for more.

carryVoice: Your line: not everything. Income matters, often a great deal, and it's still not everything. See you tomorrow.
